questions.q: What three jobs make up log shipping, per this lesson?
options: A backup job on the primary, a copy job on the secondary, and a restore job on the secondary
A single job that both backs up and restores automatically
A backup job, an index rebuild job, and a statistics update job
A replication job, a snapshot job, and a distribution job
questions.explain: Log shipping chains three independent SQL Server Agent jobs: backup (primary), copy (secondary), restore (secondary).

questions.q: Why is log shipping resilient to a transient network hiccup between primary and secondary?
options: Each job runs on its own independent schedule, so the copy job simply catches up on its next run
It uses synchronous replication that blocks until the network recovers
It has no network dependency at all
SQL Server automatically reroutes traffic through a different network path
questions.explain: Because backup, copy, and restore each run independently on their own schedules, a temporary gap is simply caught up on the next scheduled run.

questions.q: What does restoring log backups WITH NORECOVERY do to the secondary database?
options: Leaves it inaccessible for querying, in a restoring state ready for the next log restore
Makes it immediately available for read-write queries
Makes it read-only but queryable between restores
Deletes the secondary database entirely
questions.explain: WITH NORECOVERY keeps the database in a restoring state, appropriate when the secondary exists purely to fail over to.

questions.q: What is the real tradeoff of using WITH STANDBY instead of WITH NORECOVERY on the secondary?
options: The secondary becomes queryable between restores, but active readers are briefly disconnected each time the next log restore runs
There is no tradeoff — STANDBY is strictly better in every scenario
STANDBY makes the secondary fully read-write
STANDBY eliminates the need for a restore job entirely
questions.explain: STANDBY allows read-only querying between restores, at the cost of disconnecting readers briefly during each restore.

questions.q: How far behind the primary is a log shipping secondary, realistically, compared to an Availability Group's synchronous replica?
options: Minutes behind, based on the backup/copy/restore schedule — not seconds like a synchronous AG replica
Exactly the same latency as a synchronous AG replica
Log shipping has zero latency because it streams continuously
Log shipping is always faster than any AG replica
questions.explain: Because each job runs on a schedule rather than streaming continuously, log shipping's latency is realistically measured in minutes, unlike a synchronous AG replica.
